paragraphs.heading: Pictures made from shaking
paragraphs.text: Seismic tomography is a way of making images of what lies beneath Earth's surface by using seismic waves. Most often those waves come from earthquakes, or from man-made sources such as explosions. The material a wave passes through changes the wave's properties. By comparing how the waves recorded at different places differ from one another, scientists can build a model of the structure below.

paragraphs.heading: What the image shows
paragraphs.text: The result is almost always a model of seismic velocity, the speed of the waves. If Earth were made of the same stuff throughout, seismic waves would move in straight lines. Differences in structure, chemistry and temperature change the waves, above all their velocity, and this causes the waves to be reflected and refracted. Features in the finished model may then be read as variations in structure, temperature or composition. Geoscientists use the method at scales that range from the whole Earth down to the top few meters below the surface.

paragraphs.heading: Working backward from the data
paragraphs.text: Tomography is solved as an inverse problem. Scientists begin with a starting model of Earth and compare the seismic data against it. They then keep changing the model until its predictions match the observations as closely as possible. This process can work out where the variations underground are and how large they are, although the solutions are not unique. Most commonly only the travel time of the waves is used. Better modeling and more computing power now allow parts of the recorded waveform, or all of it, to be fitted as well.

paragraphs.heading: Like a CT scan, but harder
paragraphs.text: The method resembles a medical CT scan, in that a computer turns data from receivers into a 3D image. There are differences. A CT scan uses attenuation where seismic tomography uses differences in travel time. A CT scan also works with linear x-rays and a known source. Seismic tomography has to cope with ray paths that curve, reflecting and refracting inside the Earth, and the location of the earthquake that produced the waves may be uncertain.

paragraphs.heading: How the method took shape
paragraphs.text: In the early 20th century, seismologists first used variations in the travel times of earthquake waves to make discoveries such as the depth to the outer core. Modern tomography was not developed until the 1970s, as global seismic networks expanded. A 1976 paper, the earliest widely cited one that largely resembles the modern method, used local earthquakes to work out the 3D velocity structure under Southern California. The next year, delay times of P waves were turned into 2D velocity maps of the whole Earth at several ranges of depth.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name came from
paragraphs.text: In 1984 came the first model built with iterative techniques. These improve on a starting model in small steps, and they are needed when the number of unknowns is large. The same study was the first to use the word "tomography" in seismology. The term had begun in medicine, with X-ray tomography.

paragraphs.heading: Limits of the image
paragraphs.text: Waves with longer wavelengths reach deeper into the Earth. The catch is that a seismic wave cannot pick out features much smaller than its own wavelength, so these waves give a lower resolution. Different methods also rest on different assumptions, and that can strongly affect the picture. Commonly used methods work by improving an input model step by step, so an unreasonable starting model can lead to unrealistic results.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond simple rays
paragraphs.text: Historically, seismic waves have been modeled as 1D rays, an approach known as ray theory. It is fairly simple and can usually fit travel-time data well. Yet a recorded waveform holds far more information than travel time alone, and it is shaped by a much wider path than ray theory assumes. A more recent approach, called full waveform tomography, drops ray theory altogether. It models the spread of seismic waves in its full complexity and can give more accurate images of the subsurface.
